p.src: Now, in the ninth month of autumn, the sixth year of Jianxing in Shu-Han, the Wei commander Cao Xiu was utterly defeated by Lu Xun of Eastern Wu at Shiting, losing all his carriages, horses, military supplies, and equipment. Cao Xiu was so stricken with fear and shame that anxiety made him ill. On reaching Luoyang, an ulcer broke out on his back and he died; the Wei emperor Cao Rui ordered that he be buried with full honors. Sima Yi led his army back. The generals came out to receive him and asked, “Commander Cao’s defeat concerns you directly as commander-in-chief. Why have you hurried back?” Sima Yi replied, “I expect Zhuge Liang, learning of our defeat, will exploit the opening and come to seize Chang’an. If Longxi should face an emergency, who would come to its rescue? That is why I returned.” They all took him for a coward, and withdrew with derisive laughter.

p.src: Meanwhile, Eastern Wu sent an envoy with a letter to Shu, requesting troops for a campaign against Wei and reporting Cao Xiu’s crushing defeat—first to display its own might, and second to strengthen the goodwill of the alliance. The Latter Emperor was delighted and ordered the letter taken to Hanzhong to inform Kongming. At the time, Kongming’s troops were strong, his horses fit, his stores of grain and fodder plentiful, and everything needed for war fully prepared; he was just about to launch the expedition. On hearing this news, he at once gave a banquet for all the generals and discussed the campaign with them. Suddenly a great wind rose from the northeast and snapped a pine tree before the hall. Everyone was greatly alarmed. Kongming immediately cast a divination and said, “This wind foretells the loss of a great general!” The generals did not believe him. While they were still drinking, word suddenly came that Zhao Tong and Zhao Guang, the elder and younger sons of General Who Guards the South Zhao Yun, had arrived to see the chancellor. Kongming was aghast. Casting his cup to the ground, he cried, “Zilong is no more!” The two sons entered, bowed, and wept: “Our father’s illness worsened at midnight last night, and he died.” Kongming stamped his foot and wept: “With Zilong’s death, the state has lost a pillar, and I have lost an arm!” Not one of the generals failed to shed tears. Kongming ordered the two sons to go to Chengdu, appear before the emperor, and report the death. When the Latter Emperor heard that Zhao Yun was dead, he wailed aloud: “When I was a child, had it not been for Zilong, I would have died amid the chaos of battle!” He immediately issued an edict posthumously appointing Zhao Yun Grand General, granting him the title Marquis Shunping, and ordering his burial east of Jinping Mountain in Chengdu. p.src: Meanwhile, scouts from the leading ranks of the Shu army reached Chencang and returned to report to Kongming: “A city has been built at the entrance to the Chencang road. A general named Hao Zhao is guarding it. Its moats are deep, its ramparts high, and chevaux-de-frise are set everywhere; the defenses are exceedingly strict. It would be far easier to leave this city aside, take the narrow bird-path over the Taibai Range, and emerge at Qishan.” Kongming said, “Jieting lies due north of Chencang. Only after taking this city can we advance.” He ordered Wei Yan to lead troops beneath the walls and attack from all four sides. After several days without breaching the city, Wei Yan returned and told Kongming that it was difficult to take. Kongming flew into a rage and intended to have Wei Yan beheaded. Suddenly a man below the command tent said, “Though I possess little ability, I have followed the chancellor for many years without ever repaying his favor. I ask leave to enter Chencang and persuade Hao Zhao to surrender, without our drawing a bow or loosing a single arrow.” They looked and saw that it was Yin Xiang, a subordinate officer. Kongming asked, “What will you say to persuade him?” Yin Xiang replied, “Hao Zhao and I are both natives of Longxi, and we have been close friends since childhood. When I reach him, I shall explain where his advantage and peril lie, and he is certain to surrender.” Kongming at once ordered him to go.

p.src: Yin Xiang returned and reported to Kongming, “Hao Zhao cut me off before I could even begin to speak.” Kongming said, “Go and see him again, and explain the advantage and peril to him.” Yin Xiang returned to the city wall and asked to see Hao Zhao. Hao Zhao came out onto the gate tower facing the enemy. Yin Xiang reined in his horse and called loudly, “My worthy younger brother Bodao, heed my loyal counsel. You hold one isolated city; how can you resist an army of several hundred thousand? If you do not surrender now, regret will come too late. Moreover, you refuse allegiance to the great Han and serve the usurping Wei. How can you be so blind to Heaven’s mandate and so unable to distinguish the pure from the foul? I beg you to consider it, Bodao.” Hao Zhao was furious. He took up his bow, fitted an arrow, pointed it at Yin Xiang, and shouted, “My decision was settled in what I said before. You need say no more. Withdraw at once, and I shall spare you my arrow!” Yin Xiang returned to Kongming and gave a full account of Hao Zhao’s conduct. Kongming flew into a rage. “That fellow is intolerably insolent! Does he imagine that I have no engines for attacking a city?” He immediately summoned a local man and asked, “How many troops are there in Chencang?” The local replied, “I do not know the exact number, but there are about three thousand.” Kongming laughed. “How can such a petty city withstand me? Do not wait for their reinforcements to arrive. Attack with all speed!”

p.src: The army therefore raised a hundred scaling towers. Each could hold more than ten men atop it and was shielded on all sides with wooden boards. Each soldier carried a short ladder and a rope, ready to scale the walls together when the drums sounded in the camp. From a defensive tower, Hao Zhao saw the Shu troops erect their scaling towers and approach from every side, so he ordered three thousand men to take up fire arrows and deploy around the walls; when the towers neared the walls, they were all to shoot at once. Kongming had assumed that the city was unprepared; hence he had built so many scaling towers and ordered the whole army to advance amid drums and battle cries. Unexpectedly, fire arrows flew from the walls in volleys, burning every scaling tower and many of the soldiers upon them to death. Arrows and stones rained from the walls, and the Shu troops all withdrew. Kongming said furiously, “You have burned my scaling towers; then I shall employ battering rams!” That very night he had the battering rams prepared. The next day they advanced once more from all sides, beating drums and shouting. Hao Zhao hastily ordered stones to be bored through and threaded with kudzu ropes, then swung down upon the rams, smashing them all. Kongming next ordered earth carried up to fill the moat and told Liao Hua to lead three thousand men with spades and mattocks in digging a tunnel by night, so as to enter the city secretly. Hao Zhao countered by digging deep trenches within the city to cut the tunnels off. Thus they attacked day and night for more than twenty days, yet found no means of breaking through. Kongming grew anxious and dejected. Suddenly a report came: “Relief troops have arrived from the east. Their banner reads, ‘Wang Shuang, Vanguard General of Wei.’” Kongming asked, “Who can meet him?” Wei Yan said, “I am willing to go.” Kongming replied, “You are the vanguard general and must not be lightly sent forth.” He asked again, “Who dares meet him?” The deputy general Xie Xiong immediately stepped forward. Kongming gave him three thousand troops, and he departed. Kongming asked once more, “Who else dares go?” The deputy general Gong Qi promptly volunteered. Kongming likewise gave him three thousand troops, and he departed. Fearing that Hao Zhao might lead a sortie from within the city, Kongming withdrew his forces twenty li and made camp.

p.src: Now Xie Xiong led his force onward and encountered Wang Shuang head-on. Before three bouts had passed, Wang Shuang cut him down with a single stroke. The Shu troops fled in defeat. Wang Shuang pursued close behind. Gong Qi met him, but after only three passes he too was slain by Wang Shuang. The routed soldiers returned and reported to Kongming. Greatly alarmed, Kongming hurriedly ordered Liao Hua, Wang Ping, and Zhang Yi to meet the enemy. When the two armies had drawn up facing each other, Zhang Yi rode forth. Wang Ping and Liao Hua held the flanks. Wang Shuang spurred forward and fought Zhang Yi for several passes, neither gaining the advantage. Wang Shuang feigned defeat and fled; Zhang Yi pursued him. Seeing that Zhang Yi had fallen into the trap, Wang Ping hastily cried, “Do not pursue!” As Zhang Yi hurriedly wheeled his horse, Wang Shuang’s meteor hammer had already flown and struck him squarely in the back. Zhang Yi bent over his saddle and fled, while Wang Shuang turned his horse and gave chase. Wang Ping and Liao Hua intercepted Wang Shuang and rescued Zhang Yi back to their lines. Wang Shuang drove his troops forward in a great slaughter, inflicting heavy losses upon the Shu army. Zhang Yi vomited several mouthfuls of blood, returned to Kongming, and said, “Wang Shuang is a peerless warrior. His twenty thousand troops are now encamped outside Chencang, with palisades on every side, multiple ramparts raised, and deep trenches dug; their defenses are exceedingly strict.” Seeing that two generals had been lost and Zhang Yi wounded, Kongming summoned Jiang Wei and said, “The route through Chencang cannot be taken. What other plan have you?” Jiang Wei replied, “Chencang’s walls are strong, and Hao Zhao’s defenses are exceedingly thorough; with Wang Shuang now assisting him, the city truly cannot be taken. It would be better to order a senior general to establish a fortified camp with mountains and water at his back; then Cao Zhen can be captured.” Kongming followed his advice and immediately ordered Wang Ping and Li Hui to lead two thousand troops in guarding the byroad at Jieting; Wei Yan was to lead a force in guarding the entrance to Chencang. Ma Dai was made vanguard, while Guan Xing and Zhang Bao were assigned to support the front and rear. They emerged from the bypath through Xie Valley and advanced toward Mount Qi.

The man said, “I am no spy. I came bearing secret intelligence for the Commander but was mistakenly seized by the troops lying in ambush along the road. I beg you to dismiss the attendants.”
Cao Zhen had his bonds removed, and the attendants temporarily withdrew.
The man said, “I am a trusted servant of Jiang Boyue and have been sent by my lord to deliver a secret letter.”
Cao Zhen asked, “Where is the letter?”
The man drew it from beneath the clothing next to his skin and presented it. Cao Zhen broke the seal and read:

p.src: After reading it, Cao Zhen exclaimed in delight, “Heaven has granted me this victory!” He richly rewarded the messenger and sent him back with instructions to meet as appointed. Cao Zhen summoned Fei Yao to confer and said, “Jiang Wei has secretly sent me a letter proposing such and such a plan.” Fei Yao replied, “Zhuge Liang is full of stratagems, and Jiang Wei is richly endowed with cunning. This may have been done at Zhuge Liang’s command; I fear there is deception within it.” Cao Zhen said, “He was originally a man of Wei and surrendered to Shu only because he had no choice. Why should we doubt him?” Fei Yao replied, “Commander, you must not advance rashly; remain here and hold the main camp. I am willing to lead a force to support Jiang Wei. If the venture succeeds, the credit shall belong to you; if it proves a treacherous scheme, I shall answer for it myself.” Cao Zhen was delighted and ordered Fei Yao to lead fifty thousand troops toward Xie Valley. After two or three stages, Fei Yao encamped his troops and sent out scouts. At about the hour of the monkey that day, a scout returned and reported, “Shu troops are coming through Xie Valley.” Fei Yao hurriedly urged his troops forward. Before battle was joined, the Shu troops withdrew. Fei Yao ordered a pursuit; the Shu troops returned, but just as the armies were about to engage, they withdrew again. This happened three times. Thus they were delayed until the hour of the monkey on the following day. For a day and a night, the Wei army had not dared rest, fearing an attack by the Shu troops. Just as they were about to halt and cook, tremendous shouts suddenly arose on every side, drums and horns sounded together, and Shu troops came flooding over hill and field. The command banners parted, revealing a four-wheeled carriage in which Kongming sat upright. He sent a man to invite the Wei commander to parley. Fei Yao rode out. Seeing Kongming from afar, he secretly rejoiced and turned to those around him, saying, “If the Shu troops close in, retreat at once. If you see fire rise behind the mountain, turn back and attack; troops will be there to support us.” After giving these instructions, Fei Yao rode forward and cried, “You who were defeated before—why have you come chasing after us again?” Kongming replied, “Call Cao Zhen out to speak with me!” Fei Yao cursed him, saying, “Commander Cao is of the imperial blood. How could he consent to meet a rebel?”

p.src: Kongming flew into a rage and signaled with a sweep of his feather fan. Ma Dai charged out with one force on the left, and Zhang Yi with another on the right. The Wei troops immediately retreated. Before they had gone thirty li, they saw flames rising behind the Shu forces and heard battle cries resounding without cease. Two forces came charging out, Guan Xing on the left and Zhang Bao on the right. From the mountains above, arrows and stones rained down upon them. The Wei army suffered a crushing defeat. Realizing that he had fallen into a trap, Fei Yao rallied his retreating troops and fled toward a mountain valley, but both men and horses were exhausted. From behind, Guan Xing pursued them with fresh troops. The Wei soldiers trampled one another or plunged into ravines to their deaths, beyond all counting. Fei Yao fled for his life, only to encounter a body of troops at the mouth of a mountain slope. Their commander was Jiang Wei. Fei Yao cursed him: “Faithless rebel! To my misfortune, I have been deceived by your treacherous scheme!” Jiang Wei laughed and said, “I meant to capture Cao Zhen, but ensnared you by mistake. Dismount at once and surrender!” Fei Yao spurred his horse, forced a way through, and fled into the mountain valley. Suddenly he saw flames soaring skyward within the valley, while the pursuing troops again closed in from behind. Fei Yao cut his own throat and died, and all his remaining men surrendered. Kongming drove his army onward through the night, marched straight to the foot of Mount Qi, established camp, settled his troops, and richly rewarded Jiang Wei. Jiang Wei said, “My only regret is that I could not kill Cao Zhen.” Kongming likewise said, “It is a pity that so grand a scheme yielded so small a prize.”

p.src: Now Cao Zhen, learning that Fei Yao had been lost, regretted his decision when it was already too late. He therefore consulted Guo Huai about a plan for retreat. Sun Li and Xin Pi immediately prepared a memorial by night and submitted it to the ruler of Wei, reporting that the Shu army had again emerged at Mount Qi, that Cao Zhen had lost troops and commanders, and that the situation was extremely perilous. Cao Rui was greatly alarmed. He immediately summoned Sima Yi into his presence and said, “Cao Zhen has lost troops and commanders, and the Shu army has again emerged at Mount Qi. What plan have you to drive it back?” Sima Yi replied, “Your servant already has a plan to drive back Zhuge Liang. There will be no need for the Wei army to brandish its might or display its power; the Shu troops will withdraw of their own accord.” Indeed:
